newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan rejects U.S. charges on trade barriers.
newsitem.headline: Japan rejects U.S. charges on trade barriers.

text.p: Japan on Wednesday rejected U.S. charges that Tokyo has trade barriers that thwart sales of foreign goods, arguing that Washington must redress its own trade barriers before criticising Japan.

The rejection was contained in a 47-page report which the Japanese government submitted to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) on Wednesday in response to a USTR report on global trade barriers released in late March.
The 381-page USTR report devoted some 45 pages to Japan, where the USTR said problems involving a number of business sectors remain despite 24 trade agreements since 1992.

"The (U.S.) report takes an inappropriate approach that is result-oriented, making distorted decisions as to the existence of market barriers and the extent to which market access is growing," the Japanese report said.

Japan said Washington is not entitled to criticise Japan for retaining high tariffs on certain products as the tariff rates are the outcome of the Uruguay Round of global trade talks and are all consistent with a World Trade Organisation accord.
"Before the U.S. criticises Japan, it should become sufficiently aware of the fact of its own high tariffs and redress these first," the Japanese report said.

U.S. officials have urged Japan to open its markets to American firms. "I believe we must continue to push Japan to adopt policies that favour domestic-led growth and to deregulate its economy in market-opening ways," Robert Reis, an acting deputy assistant secretary of state, told a Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee on Tuesday.
The Japanese report brushed aside a U.S. view that Japanese telecoms giant Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp discriminates against foreign suppliers in procuring equipment.
The Japanese report said the U.S. report lacks an analysis as to whether foreign firms are making appropriate sales efforts, and whether foreign firms offer competitive products.
"The U.S. report includes no analysis of the relevant supplier-related factors, and is thus one-sided, simplistic and inaccurate," the Japanese report said.

Last month, U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said in a statement accompanying the U.S. report that "NTT is still captive to its monopoly legacy and not fully responsive to market principles".
